title: Navin Ramgoolam
excerpt: Why does Navin Ramgoolam still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism.
author: Dr. Marcus Vance

body.text: Why does Navin Ramgoolam still shape capital allocation and market pricing across global desks? Behind the headline numbers lies a structural mechanism that quietly governs liquidity, risk, and long-term purchasing power.

Navinchandra Ramgoolam (born 14 July 1947) is a Mauritian politician, physician and barrister who has been Prime Minister of Mauritius since November 2024, an office he previously held from 1995 to 2000 and from 2005 to 2014. He has led the Labour Party since 1991 and has also been Minister of Finance since 2024.

The son of Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, who led Mauritius to independence in 1968 and was its first prime minister, he trained as a doctor in Dublin and worked in hospitals in Ireland, England and Mauritius before reading law at the London School of Economics and being called to the bar in 1993.

Ramgoolam became Labour's leader and Leader of the Opposition in 1991. In alliance with Paul Bérenger's Mauritian Militant Movement (MMM), Labour won every seat on the island of Mauritius at the 1995 general election.

body.text: His first government replaced the sales tax with value-added tax, legislated against domestic violence and for a national human rights commission, provided for private broadcasting and hosted the launch of the Indian Ocean Rim Association, while the economy grew by an average of more than five per cent a year.

The coalition with the MMM ended in 1997, the riots that followed the death in police custody of the singer Kaya tested the government in 1999, and Labour was heavily defeated by an alliance of the Militant Socialist Movement (MSM) and the MMM in 2000.
Returning to power in 2005 at the head of the Alliance Sociale, Ramgoolam governed through the loss of preferential access for Mauritian textiles and sugar.

His finance minister, Rama Sithanen, replaced a complex tax system with a flat rate of 15 per cent, abolished most investment-incentive schemes, opened the economy to foreign investors and skilled workers and restructured the sugar industry, reforms that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) commended.

3 per cent a year from 2006 to 2014, gross domestic product (GDP) per head nearly doubled in US dollar terms, and Mauritius was ranked first in Africa for governance and for the ease of doing business.

The second premiership also brought free bus travel for students and pensioners, the Truth and Justice Commission on slavery and indenture, the inscription of Aapravasi Ghat and Le Morne on the World Heritage List and the arbitration in which Mauritius successfully challenged the British marine protected area around the Chagos Archipelago.
Re-elected in 2010, he lost the 2014 election, and his own seat, after proposing a "Second Republic" with a directly elected president.
During ten years in opposition, provisional charges brought against him in 2015 were struck out, and in 2024 he led the Alliance du Changement to a 60, 0 victory on the island of Mauritius.

His third government published an audit of the public finances, held municipal elections for the first time in a decade, set up a constitutional review commission, began reforming the electoral system, overhauled the state pension and made Mauritius the first African country to adhere to the IMF's highest data-dissemination standard.
5 per cent in 2025, a year of record tourist arrivals and foreign investment, before slowing in 2026 as conflict in the Middle East raised energy prices.

Ramgoolam signed the 2025 treaty by which the United Kingdom recognises Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, raised relations with India to an "Enhanced Strategic Partnership" and received the first visit by a French president in three decades.
In 2026 Bérenger resigned as deputy prime minister, and in October riots set off by a police shooting led the government to impose a curfew.
Early life and education

Ramgoolam was born in Port Louis on 14 July 1947, the son of Seewoosagur Ramgoolam and his wife, Sushil. His father, the leader of the Labour Party and of the movement for independence, was prime minister from independence in 1968 until 1982.

Navin Ramgoolam was educated at the Royal College Curepipe from 1960 to 1968 and went on to study medicine at the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland in Dublin, where he qualified in 1975 with the licentiates of the Royal Colleges of Physicians and of Surgeons in Ireland.
After internships at St Laurence's Hospital in Dublin and at Monaghan County Hospital, he was a resident medical officer at Dr A. Jeetoo Hospital in Port Louis in 1976, 77.

He then spent most of the following decade in England: he was a clinical assistant in cardiology at University College Hospital, London, from 1977 to 1981, held locum and house-officer posts, and was resident medical officer at the Yorkshire Clinic in Bingley from 1982 to 1985, before practising as a general practitioner in Mauritius from 1985 to 1987.

His mother died on 5 January 1984, and it was at his father's death in December 1985 that Navin Ramgoolam began to appear in public life. According to Agence France-Presse, the Labour Party sought him out in order to capitalise on his father's name, he has said that he entered politics par accident ("by accident").
In 1987 he returned to London to read law at the London School of Economics, graduating with an LLB (Hons) in 1990.

He took the bar vocational course at the Inns of Court School of Law in 1992, 93, was called to the bar by the Inner Temple in 1993 and practised briefly at Thomas More Chambers in London in 1994, by which time he was already Leader of the Opposition in Mauritius.
Rise to the Labour leadership (1990, 1995)

Ramgoolam made his political debut in 1990 at the head of the campaign against the bill by which the government of Anerood Jugnauth, an alliance of the MSM and the MMM, sought to make Mauritius a republic, the government fell one vote short of the three-quarters majority needed to amend the constitution.

On 24 February 1991 Satcam Boolell handed him the leadership of the Labour Party. At the general election of 15 September 1991, at which the opposition alliance of Labour and the Parti Mauricien Social Démocrate (PMSD) won only three seats, he was elected for Constituency No.

5 (Pamplemousses, Triolet), one of three Labour members returned, and became Leader of the Opposition. He continued his legal studies in London, and in January 1993 the government majority tried to have his seat declared vacant because of his absences, the Supreme Court described the manoeuvre as a "colourable device", and he kept his seat.
After the MSM, MMM coalition broke up in 1993, Ramgoolam and Bérenger formed the Labour, MMM alliance with which they contested the next election.

He was sworn in as prime minister on 27 December 1995 and named his cabinet three days later, with Bérenger as deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs. The alliance had promised to continue the market-oriented economic policies of its predecessors while giving higher priority to social welfare.
Economy and reforms

Rundheersing Bheenick, the government's first finance minister, held the post until August 1996 and later became minister of economic development, Vasant Bunwaree was finance minister by 1997. The government's main fiscal reform was the replacement of the sales tax by a value-added tax, levied at 10 per cent from 7 September 1998.

1 per cent a year from 1996 to 1998, driven, according to the IMF, by the manufactures of the export processing zone, sugar exports and tourism, while the budget deficit narrowed from 6¼ per cent of GDP in 1995, 96 to about 3⅔ per cent in 1997, 98.
2 per cent in 2000, and consumer-price inflation stayed between about 4 and 7 per cent a year throughout the term. 0 per cent in 2000.

The Protection from Domestic Violence Act, partly in force in 1997 and fully in 1998, made domestic violence a criminal offence, and the Protection of Human Rights Act 1998 provided for a National Human Rights Commission, the act took effect in 1999, although the commission had not yet been constituted by the end of 2000.
